title: A library of sutras
hook: the Mahayana sutras are many; we read a handful, paraphrased

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Buddha reached out his hand and handed the Lotus over. Your line: entrusted.

"Thus have I heard." That's how the discourses open in the old English of Rhys Davids, before anyone is named, before a place or a crowd. For weeks this path has stayed inside one book, the Lotus. Today i'm stepping out of it with you to look at the shelf it sits on. It's a long shelf. The Mahayana sutras are many, kept in Sanskrit, Chinese and Tibetan, and loved in different places for different reasons. Over the coming weeks i'll open a handful.
screen: `THUS HAVE I HEARD.` → `ONE BOOK ON A LONG SHELF.` → `A HANDFUL, OPENED.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. A sutra is a discourse: a teaching set in a scene, with a place, a crowd, and someone asking a question. Tradition says that after the Buddha died, his attendant Ananda recited what he had heard, which is why the discourses open with those words. The Mahayana sutras open the same way, and then the scenes grow huge: assemblies of bodhisattvas, light pouring from the Buddha's brow, worlds beyond counting. Different Buddhists hold these books differently, so here, plainly, is who holds what. Mahayana traditions in China, Tibet, Korea, Japan and Vietnam receive these sutras as the Buddha's word. The Theravada tradition of Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia keeps its own canon in Pali, and these Mahayana sutras aren't part of it. Historians tell their own story about when and where the texts were written. This path tells each text as it tells itself, and names the differences without ranking anyone. Now the shelf ahead. A sick layman in the city of Vaishali who out-talks the Buddha's great disciples, and a goddess who scatters flowers in his room. A sutra that pictures the universe as a net of jewels, and a young pilgrim who visits teacher after teacher. A finger pointing at the moon. A Buddha of medicine, a bodhisattva who vows to empty the hells, and a queen named Srimala who teaches. One honest note: i'll mostly retell these in my own words, because the English translations i'd want to quote aren't ones i can share freely. When i paraphrase, i'll say so.
screen: `A SUTRA IS A DISCOURSE IN A SCENE.` · `THUS HAVE I HEARD: ANANDA'S WORDS.` · `WHO HOLDS THESE BOOKS, AND HOW.` · `THE SHELF AHEAD.` · then, large: `A LIBRARY.`

segments.voice: Say those four words silently once: thus have I heard. Notice that they don't claim to be clever; they say, I was there, and I'm passing on what reached me. Then sit the way you'd sit at the start of a story, listening, and let the sounds in the room be the opening scene.
A library of sutras. Many discourses, each opening with thus have I heard, held differently by different Buddhists. Today's word.
Your line: a library. Every book on it begins by saying where it came from. Eleven hundred eighty-five days, and counting.

howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists in East Asia, Tibet and Vietnam chant, study and copy sutras such as the Lotus, the Heart Sutra and the Vimalakirti, and each school tends to center a few of them; the Theravada tradition keeps the Pali canon instead.

chat.says: Do all Buddhists treat these Mahayana sutras as the Buddha's own words?
options: No. Mahayana traditions do; Theravada keeps its own Pali canon, and these aren't in it.
Yes. Every Buddhist school reads the same sutras as the Buddha's own word.
No. Only Tibet still uses them; China and Japan set them aside long ago.
